item.title: SALES: 11 Taos Airbnbs That Embody the Soul of the Southwest
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
From the first time my parents’ car crested the last hill on New Mexico State Road 68 en route to Taos, and the depths of the Rio Grande Gorge emerged in view, I was hooked. As a New Mexican, I’ve spent more than 30 years visiting the northern New Mexico town of Taos, where I enjoy dining on local cuisine, browsing contemporary art galleries, hiking the peaks around Taos Ski Valley, and rafting the Rio Grande rapids. As time has passed, the town’s unique charm has remained, but its popularity has only grown. Indigenous peoples have inhabited the lands here since time immemorial, and today, the residents of Taos Pueblo welcome visitors to a stacked-adobe village whose architecture is synonymous with the Southwest. Creatives have long felt called to this area, from the likes of Ansel Adams, who turned his lens on the wide buttresses of St. Francisco de Assisi Mission Church, to Georgia O’Keeffe, who first visited in 1929. One of the best ways to take in the local culture and enjoy the architecture is by staying in a Taos Airbnb. In this way, travelers get the chance to embrace elements of the town’s character, from its regional design to its counter-culture scene captured in the sustainable Earthships dotting the vast sagebrush mesa beneath mountain peaks. Whether you’re following your creative muse, want to embrace the desert landscape, or are eager to get a taste of Southwestern living, these are the best Taos Airbnbs to visit right now. item.title: REVIEW: EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus Review: Serious Output, Surprising Portability
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus ($2,199) occupies a middle ground between a portable power station and a permanent home backup system. Featuring a 3,072Wh LiFePO4 battery, support for up to 1,600W of solar input, and expandability to 11kWh, it's considerably more capable than the average portable model. Its 3,600W inverter provides enough output for demanding appliances and power tools, while a 30A connection makes it particularly interesting for RV and home backup applications. This is strictly a 120V system, meaning it won't directly operate 240V appliances such as many electric water heaters, well pumps, dryers, or central air-conditioning systems. Ultimately, the Bluetti Elite 300 ($1,699) remains our Editors’ Choice for portable power stations, offering nearly the same battery capacity in a package that weighs about 17 pounds less, though the EcoFlow’s higher output and expandability make it a compelling alternative for more demanding needs. The Delta 3 Ultra Plus ships securely in a double cardboard box, held in place by two large pieces of heavy foam. Despite its nearly 75-pound weight, getting it unpacked and on the floor was relatively easy. The station arrived with around a 50% charge and was essentially ready to use. The setup consists of extending the telescoping handle, rolling it into position, connecting the supplied AC charging cable, and powering it on. The display immediately shows the current charge level, input and output power, and estimated remaining battery life. You can use the Delta 3 Ultra Plus without the EcoFlow app (available for Android and iOS), but connecting it provides additional control over charging, outputs, and other power-management settings. There are no QR codes on the station directing you to support resources or app downloads, something the Bluetti Elite 300 arrives with. The Delta 3 Ultra Plus measures 24.14 by 12.9 by 15.55 inches (HWD) and weighs roughly 75 pounds. EcoFlow has done an excellent job of making that bulk manageable. The enclosure feels exceptionally solid, with tight panel gaps, substantial plastics, and excellent overall fit and finish. By comparison, the Bluetti Elite 300 measures 14.4 by 12 by 11.7 inches and weighs about 58 pounds, making it easier to fit into a packed vehicle and less cumbersome to lift. It also looks unusually good for a 3kWh power station. The sculpted dark gray enclosure, clean surfaces, and large display give it a modern, futuristic aesthetic with a distinctly cyber feel. It looks equally at home in my office, living room, or kitchen, which matters for a backup system you may leave in your living space. The large front display is bright and easy to read from several feet away, clearly showing battery level, remaining battery life, input and output power, and operating status. Large cooling vents are neatly integrated into the sides without making the station look overly industrial. Large side handles provide secure lifting points, but the telescoping handle and integrated wheels are what make the Delta 3 Ultra Plus genuinely manageable. The handle extends well above the chassis, providing plenty of leverage, while the wheels roll smoothly enough that moving the station feels remarkably similar to wheeling carry-on luggage through an airport. That changes the experience of owning something this heavy. Around my house, office, and garage, I rarely needed to lift it. You'll still appreciate a second set of hands when loading it into a vehicle or carrying it up stairs, but on level ground, I found that its weight largely disappears behind the handle and wheels. The Delta 3 Ultra Plus has one of the more comprehensive collections of AC and DC connections I've seen on a portable power station, sensibly divided between the front and rear. Frequently used connections face forward, while charging, expansion, solar, and higher-current DC connections are found around the back. Up front are four standard 120V AC outlets and a 30A TT-30R RV outlet that can draw power from the 3,600W inverter. The AC outlets are split into two independently controlled zones, each with its own power button. This lets you shut down one group while keeping another active, which is useful for prioritizing critical loads or simply turning off devices you don't need. There’s a setting in the app that lets you prioritize the banks, shutting down non-critical loads once the battery draws down to a level you specify while keeping critical things, like a refrigerator, running on the priority bank. EcoFlow also provides three USB-C ports and one USB-A port. The primary USB-C connection delivers up to 140W, while the other two provide up to 45W each. The USB-A port supports up to 18W. Clearly marked buttons let you activate only the output sections you're using. I wish there were at least two 140W USB-C ports, as my wife and I will both power our laptops when sitting close, or in case I want to power a laptop and a Starlink Mini ($599) simultaneously. The rear is particularly well designed. Charging and DC connections are hidden behind protective sliding doors that disappear back into the chassis when opened. You expose the ports only when you need them, then slide the covers closed to protect them from dust, dirt, and accidental contact. It's a much cleaner solution than the dangling rubber covers commonly found on portable power stations. The AC charging input can accept up to 1,800W from a standard 120V outlet. Charging speed can also be adjusted through the EcoFlow app, which is useful when sharing a household circuit or when maximum charging speed isn't necessary. Flipping the switch to fast enables maximum AC charge, while pushing it to the right sets the adjustable, app-controlled value. I set mine to 200W in the app. Two independent solar/DC inputs can each accept up to 800W for a combined 1,600W. Each supports 11V to 60V and up to 18A, allowing separate solar arrays or compatible DC charging sources to operate simultaneously. The 60V ceiling does require some attention when configuring larger panels in series, since it's relatively easy to exceed. I tested both ports by connecting 40V solar panels, including EcoFlow's 400W Portable Solar Panel ($699). To connect two of these panels in series would bring me to 80V, above the limits of the MPPT controller being used, which would damage the unit. I think EcoFlow missed an opportunity to include a 100+ V port bank, which would make it easier to connect panels in series. It’s a small sacrifice, though, considering all the other ports there are. It’s a silver Swiss Army knife on wheels. For 12V equipment, there's a conventional automotive socket rated at roughly 10A and a much more capable Anderson connector rated at up to 30A. The latter is particularly useful for RVs, overlanding, amateur radio, and other high-current DC equipment, where a cigarette-lighter socket can quickly become the limiting factor. I use portable 12V-powered diesel heaters when camping, and their initial power-draw surge exceeds traditional 12V sockets (about 150W). I wish other companies like Jackery, with their portable HomePower 2000 Plus v2 ($1,889), would adopt that high-power port as standard. In my Land Cruiser, I use the Anderson port on the EcoFlow Delta 3 Max Plus ($1,899) to power my Yaesu FT-891 HF ham radio, which draws 100+ watts on high power, tripping the fuses in standard 12V sockets. Seeing this port across multiple models was very encouraging; it feels like EcoFlow is listening to user input. I could easily see the Ultra Plus in the back of an SUV or overlanding vehicle. Finally, the expansion port allows additional EcoFlow batteries to increase storage from the native 3,072Wh to as much as 11kWh. With dual AC zones, a 30A RV outlet, high-output USB-C, dual solar inputs, and a high-current DC output, EcoFlow offers considerably more flexibility than the basic 3,600W inverter specification suggests. Specifications are useful, but I care much more about what happens when I start plugging actual appliances into a power station. The Delta 3 Ultra Plus' 3,600W inverter puts it into serious territory, with enough continuous output to operate multiple household appliances, power tools, refrigerators, and RV equipment simultaneously. For my high-load test, I skipped the laboratory resistive load and connected a space heater, two hair dryers, and a 1,000W water heater. I progressively added loads until the Delta 3 Ultra Plus was delivering approximately 3,500W continuously, just 100W shy of its 3,600W rating. When it hit that number, the heater had boiled the water in the thermos, which was spilling near the hair dryers, and I was kind of in awe of how much power the cyber station was putting out. These aren't carefully controlled laboratory loads. They're high-wattage appliances people actually use, often several at once during an outage. Microwaves, toaster ovens, washing machines. That's roughly 97% of its rated continuous output, demonstrating that the 3,600W specification isn't simply an impressive number printed on the case. That’s “life doesn’t stop because of a data center brownout” power. That much output also changes how you can use a power station during an outage. With smaller systems, I'm constantly doing mental arithmetic before turning on another high-draw appliance. Here, there's enough inverter capacity to operate several substantial 120V loads simultaneously without playing musical chairs with the outlets. Capacity is another matter. The Delta 3 Ultra Plus has a rated battery capacity of 3,072Wh, but you won't get all of that energy from the AC outlets. Some is inevitably lost converting the battery's DC power into 120V AC, running the electronics, and maintaining the system's protective reserve. The Bluetti Elite 300’s rated 3,014Wh capacity is less than 2% lower, despite its smaller, lighter design. The EcoFlow’s larger enclosure buys you greater continuous output—3,600W versus 2,400W—but very little additional capacity unless you add expansion batteries. Instrumented testing measured 2,630Wh of usable AC energy before shutdown, or about 85.6% of the rated battery capacity. In practical terms, roughly 14% of the energy stored in the battery never reaches the connected AC appliance. That's why simply dividing 3,072Wh by an appliance's wattage will usually yield an overly optimistic battery life estimate. Idle consumption matters as well, particularly when powering appliances that cycle on and off. With the AC inverter enabled but nothing connected, testing showed the battery dropping from 100% to 91% over 12 hours, or about 0.75% per hour. That's approximately 23Wh of stored energy every hour just to keep the AC side awake. The DC side performed somewhat better, delivering 2,653Wh of usable energy, or 86.3% of rated capacity, while consuming only around 0.25% per hour at idle. Refrigerator Testing: Up to Two Days of Cold Food Of course, powering a pile of hair dryers isn't how most people will use the Delta 3 Ultra Plus. One of my most important real-world tests remains something far less dramatic: Keeping a refrigerator running. Watching several hundred dollars of food in the freezer thaw and spoil isn't good. A refrigerator is an excellent power-station test because its compressor repeatedly cycles on and off, producing short startup demands followed by long periods of relatively low consumption. It also exposes why idle consumption matters. The inverter continues consuming energy while it waits for the refrigerator compressor to cycle back on. The Delta 3 Ultra Plus had no trouble handling my refrigerator, including repeated compressor startups. Its 3,072Wh battery also provides enough capacity to make it useful during an extended outage rather than simply bridging a short interruption, and my tests averaged between 44 and 48 hours of normal usage. UPS Performance: A 10ms Safety Net for Long Jobs The Delta 3 Ultra Plus provides a claimed 10ms UPS switchover, allowing it to remain connected between utility power and important equipment when the grid disappears. This feature is particularly important in my office because I routinely run computers and large 3D printers with jobs that can continue for 24 to 48 hours or longer. A momentary interruption can mean losing an entire print, wasting material, and starting over from scratch. E-Bike Charging: Three Full Recharges, Plus Change I've also been keeping track of how well these larger power stations can recharge my e-bikes. I'm particularly interested in using solar to harvest energy during the day, store it in the power station, and effectively create an off-grid “energy gas tank” for electric transportation. My Jasion Hunter Pro ($1,999) uses a 48V, 15Ah battery with 720Wh of capacity. Based on the Delta 3 Ultra Plus' measured 2,630Wh of usable AC energy, there's theoretically enough energy for about 3.6 full battery charges. Once I account for losses through the bike's AC charger and charging process, however, roughly three full recharges is a much more realistic expectation, with some capacity left over. That makes the Delta 3 Ultra Plus particularly interesting for remote riding, camping, or emergency transportation. Rather than simply carrying enough stored energy for one more ride, I can potentially recharge the Hunter Pro several times and replenish the EcoFlow itself from solar, theoretically indefinitely. It's a practical example of how a 3kWh power station can become more than just backup power for the house. RV and Camping: Plug In Your Camper, Power Your Campsite The 30A TT-30R outlet makes the Delta 3 Ultra Plus particularly useful with my camper. Rather than running extension cords to individual appliances, I can connect the camper directly to the EcoFlow and power its electrical system just as I would from a campground pedestal. Its 3,600W inverter provides enough output to run the air conditioner or electric heater along with lower-draw loads such as lights, ventilation fans, outlets, chargers, laptops, and other electronics plugged in inside. It also makes an excellent foundation for off-grid camping because I can connect portable solar panels directly to the Delta 3 Ultra Plus and replenish the battery during the day. With up to 1,600W of solar input available, a campsite can effectively become its own miniature power grid. My biggest concern for outdoor use is that the Delta 3 Ultra Plus isn't designed to be left exposed to rain or other wet conditions. For camping, I'd plan on keeping it inside the camper, beneath an awning, or otherwise protected from the weather. One advantage EcoFlow has built over the years is an increasingly complete ecosystem around its power stations. I was able to run my EcoFlow Wave 3 ($2,199) portable air conditioner and heater from the Delta 3 Ultra Plus and connect two 400W EcoFlow folding solar panels to replenish the battery while camping. EcoFlow also offers its Glacier line of portable refrigerators, giving you the components to build a fairly complete off-grid electrical system around a single power station, as well as a smart, automatic generator that will recharge the batteries when solar input is lacking. It all connects seamlessly in the app, with each component easily recognized and added via Bluetooth. I've already found the Wave 3 particularly useful while traveling. On a ferry trip to Ocracoke, we were required to shut off the vehicle's engine for the roughly two-and-a-half-hour crossing on a day when temperatures were around 90 degrees. I powered the Wave 3 from the EcoFlow Delta 3 Max and kept the cabin at about 72 degrees for my wife and our dogs during the trip, using a DIY foam-board insulation panel to run the exhaust and fresh-air tubes out through the back window hatch. The Wave 3 has its own expansion battery with a solar input that can power the AC at maximum for nearly three hours. That's the kind of use case that makes the ecosystem more compelling to me than simply having another large battery. The Ultra Plus can serve as the central power source for cooling and heating, refrigeration, RV equipment, electronics, and other campsite loads, and can use solar to put some of that energy back into the battery when you're away from the grid. EcoFlow’s mobile app adds considerable control beyond simply checking battery level. The dashboard provides a live view of power flowing through the system, including individual solar inputs, remaining capacity, and estimated charging time. During testing, I could easily see my two solar inputs independently producing 275W and 232W, for a combined 507W. The Delta 3 Ultra Plus also features dual-zone AC output, dividing its AC outlets into two independently managed groups. Through the app, you can assign priority to one zone, so that if demand exceeds the power station's supply, it can shed lower-priority loads while keeping critical equipment powered. That could mean keeping a refrigerator, medical device, or other essential appliance running while less important loads are disconnected. Other controls include charge and discharge limits, operating modes, output port memory (allows the station to retain its previous settings after a power loss), scheduled tasks (allows the station to automatically charge your devices during off-peak hours), and X-Boost (for powering high-wattage appliances that exceed the station's rated AC output). Storm Guard can monitor severe weather and prepare the battery for an outage when connected to the grid and internet. There's also an in-app EcoFlow Assistant that can help you navigate the system’s growing collection of features. It’s a chatbot that can answer your questions about the system, and I found it surprisingly useful and informative. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus is equally at home keeping a refrigerator running through a multiday outage or powering a camper off the grid with portable solar panels. Its 3,600W inverter handled nearly its full rated load with real appliances during testing, and it adds fast 1,800W AC charging, 1,600W of solar input, a 30A RV outlet, and dual-zone AC outlets to prioritize critical equipment. At roughly 75 pounds, it’s heavy, though its wheels and telescoping handle make it easy to move. It also lacks weather protection, a notable omission for a station this well-suited to camping, and as a 120V-only system, it can't run 240V appliances. If 2,400W of output meets your needs, our Editors' Choice, the Bluetti Elite 300, offers nearly the same capacity in a lighter package for $500 less. But if you need to run several demanding appliances at once or want room to expand to 11kWh, the Delta 3 Ultra Plus is worth the extra bulk and cost. I’m a mechanical engineer with more than 30 years of experience in industrial automation and design, with projects ranging from individual inventors to international corporations. I hold credit on six patents and have never stopped looking at the world through the glasses of "What if we did this?" I’ve been 3D printing for more than 15 years, designing in Autodesk Inventor and Fusion 360, and working across both SLA and FDM printers. My fabrication background spans machining, CNC programming, welding, and brazing. I’m also an Amateur Extra Class ham radio operator (AA2QO), with a focus on portable low-power HF communications. I’m a curious Gen Xer, inspired early on by Jim Henson’s groundbreaking Creature Shop. His work showed me how imagination, engineering, and design could bring new worlds to life—a lesson I’ve carried through my career and personal passions. I live in the foothills of North Carolina’s Appalachian Mountains with my wife of 30 years. From home base, I explore in my technology-laden 2024 Toyota Land Cruiser, and when I’m not on the road, I develop predictive financial software for retail traders and investors.

item.title: SALES: Snag These 11 Fall Travel Deals Before It's Too Late
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Are you, like me, craving a Caribbean beach with a cocktail in hand? Or maybe a transatlantic cruise is calling your name? Consider these fall travel deals your excuse to start daydreaming about your next getaway. As we get closer to Thanksgiving, early Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales are starting to crop up, along with hot-off-the-press cruise offers and loads of airfare bargains worth keeping on your radar, including both international and domestic routes. Now's a great time to start comparing prices, mapping out flexibility on travel dates, and seeing what’s on offer before the holiday shopping frenzy kicks in. As for where to go, the world is your oyster. Fall is an appealing time to book for a reason—especially for those opting for last-minute trips: Many destinations are between peak summer and winter holiday travel, while cruise lines are moving ships between regions, sometimes offering repositioning itineraries that make for memorable longer voyages. After sifting through dozens of sales, here are the very best fall travel deals to work into your next itinerary. Book a last-minute Celebrity Cruise for a stellar rate Looking for a value-forward cruise to the Caribbean, Alaska, or Europe? Top-rated cruise line Celebrity Cruises offers a weekly Exciting Deals page with discounts to all of the above, and the line-up is already pretty enticing. For one? Come late November, you can sail one of Celebrity's newest ships to the ABC Islands and take up to $700 off in instant savings, and your second guest can sail for up to 75% off. A new series of these exciting deals will launch on Monday, November 2, 2026, and continue every Monday through the end of the year. Northeast sailors get up to 15% off Virgin Voyages Calling all northeast residents—your next ocean escape just got a little more tempting. Virgin Voyages is offering residents of New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Connecticut up to 15% off eligible cruise fares with its limited-time Northeast Resident Rate (which can net out to over $1,000 in savings). From sailings to Canada and New England to ones in Charleston and Bermuda, the adults-only cruise line has plenty of ways to trade your usual routine for a few days at sea. I’ve sailed from NYC to Bermuda with Virgin myself and can vouch for the fun of swapping city views for ocean breezes. Even better? All-in voyage pricing includes Wi-Fi, dining at more than 20 eateries, genuinely fun entertainment, fitness classes, and nonalcoholic drinks. The resident rate can also be combined with select promotions; just use code NORTHEASTRATE when booking and don't forget to bring proof of residency when checking in. Score up to 35% off (and more) on holiday sailings with MSC Cruises Act quick on this one, folks: MSC Cruises' holiday sale runs through November 5 and features up to 35% off select sailings, plus children 17 and younger can sail free as third or fourth guests. With trips starting at $156 for four nights, get ready for a value-forward trip of sunbathing across the Bahamas and Ocean Cay, Puerto Rico, or the British Virgin Islands. For more deals far less timely, check out the site's deals page, where MSC constantly updates new offerings, from Voyagers Club perks to last-minute cruise deals. Take advantage of Four Season's fall discounts on stays across the globe It's no secret that Four Seasons properties are absolute hotel havens in the world of travel. That said, a discount on these gems can never hurt. Through December 31, 2027, you can score a fourth night free when you book three consecutive nights at The Ocean Club in the Bahamas. If Puerto Rico is more your speed, take advantage of the Experience More spending credit of up to $500 when you book a stay of three nights or more at the Four Seasons Resort and Residences Puerto Rico. (I've been to this property and can't recommend it enough.) This promotion is valid for stays through January 4, 2027. Save even more on your travel plans with Four Seasons promo codes. Be among the first to stay at the world’s first JW Marriott All-Inclusive JW Marriott is entering the all-inclusive space for the first time this fall with the opening of JW Marriott Costa Elena Resort and Spa on Costa Rica’s Guanacaste Coast. Lucky for its first-timers, the property's Be First Experience offers up to 15% off the resort’s all-inclusive rate, plus a $150 spa credit per stay, a complimentary room upgrade, early check-in and late check-out (based on availability), and a signature JW experience for two—with a choice of a private mixology class or guided wellness journey. And it's certainly an opening to look out for: Set along a Blue Star–designated beach and surrounded by tropical dry forest, the 415-room resort will feature Costa Rica’s largest resort poolscape, JW Marriott’s largest on-property garden, 11 restaurants and bars, and a spa and wellness center. Book by the end of November for stays through December 20, and be sure to use promo code S5235. Book a fall getaway at up to 60% off with this Iberostar coupon If you’re planning to finish off 2026 in style, you may want to take advantage of Iberostar last-minute offers across the globe. Once you enter Iberostar promo code LASTMINUTE into the hotel website's discounts field—like magic—you'll save up to 60% on sun-soaked hotels this fall. In Miami, for one, you can save up to 35% on a sun-soaked stay in South Beach. Caribbean travelers can save up to 60% at Iberostar Selection Riviera Cancun, up to 50% at Iberostar Waves Costa Dorada in the Dominican Republic, and up to 45% off at the brand’s top-rated Iberostar Selection Paraíso Maya Suites. Looking for more ways to save? Check out more of Iberostar's limited time offers on its official deals page. Save even more on your travel plans with Iberostar promo codes. Save on tours and experiences when you stay with Hilton With Hilton’s latest perk, travelers can take 15% off experiences booked through GetYourGuide (including guided tours, excursions, and local activities, oh my!) when staying at participating new or newly renovated Hilton properties in top destinations like New York City, Las Vegas, Miami, and Oahu. Just book your hotel stay by December 31, 2026, for travel through March 31, 2027. Check the website to see if the city of your choice is considered a top destination—even if it’s not, all other participating global destinations still receive a 10% discount. Snag up to 30% off last-minute tours with G Adventures If you’ve got a sudden urge to get up and go, G Adventures has hundreds of last-minute travel deals with up to 30% off tours departing in the next 60 days. We’re talking discounts off some of their most-loved and top-rated trips, including Northern Thailand: Hilltribes and Villages and chasing Costa Rica: Coastlines and Clouds Forests. If your schedule’s flexible and your passport’s ready, this is the kind of deal you jump on before it disappears. Score up to 25% off on Hertz rental cars in Canada and the US We're in the thick of fall travel, and Hertz is making it easy to hit the road. Book by the end of November to save up to 25% on base rates at participating locations all across Canada and the US for travel through the rest of the year. Whether you’re chasing snow-capped mountains or solitude in a charming small town, this is the perfect excuse to plan a road trip. (Though, do note that the deal is subject to availability, so double check your dates before booking a trip around it.) Book discounted flights around the world with Expedia Expedia's November Flight Deals page is making it easy to find discounted flights. If you want a quick getaway before the winter chaos hits, Expedia's Air Hacks data argues that you don't have to book months in advance to score deals: The sweet spot for domestic airfare is actually a tight 15 to 30 days before departure, meaning last-minute planners get an automatic advantage. That said, if you're booking Thanksgiving travel, be sure to secure your seats on Expedia by November 5 to save up to $125. You can also score on international airfare when booking on Expedia, with off-season pricing on flights to destinations like Mérida or Brazil (and you'll get there before the crowds do). Bundle and save on domestic travel with Southwest Airlines Southwest Airlines has teamed up with MGM Resorts to launch Getaways by Southwest, offering travelers significant savings on flight and hotel packages. Jet-setters looking to explore major domestic destinations can save up to $250 on select five-night domestic packages, while international travelers heading to hot spots like Cancun and Punta Cana can slash up to $500 off select bookings of five nights or more. Whether you are aiming for the bright lights of Las Vegas, the beaches of Hawaii, or a tropical Mexican escape, this partnership bundles your essential travel needs into a single, budget-friendly price. item.title: REVIEW: Astell & Kern PD5 review: the most 'sensible' player yet from A&K visually —but sonically it soars above the competition
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
It’s not cheap (despite what Astell & Kern would have you believe) but in terms of sound quality the PD5 is worth every penny. Pair it with similarly capable headphones, concentrate on the sound rather than the look or the feel, and ignore its (very) occasionally glitchy operation, and it’s a really rewarding device. - +Staggeringly clean, open and revealing sound - -Looks and feels less premium than the price demands Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. It’s been a long time since Astell & Kern has had a genuinely affordable digital audio player in its line-up, and the launch of the PD5 does nothing to change that. It’s been a while since the company had anything as visually unremarkable as this in its catalog, too — but try not to get hung up on the perceived value and instead concentrate on the priceless nature of its sound quality. And besides, a considerable amount of money put Astell & Kern’s way for a PD5 may not buy you much in the way of design or tactility but it gets you an extremely thoroughly specified device. Eight Cirrus Logic DACs? 20-point EQ adjustment? Balanced and unbalanced headphone outputs? The ability to work as a desktop DAC? Enough power to get a tune out even the most uncooperative headphones? The PD5 has all of this, and more — and it’s all in the service of audio performance that’s as good as any portable device at anything like this price point. When it comes to clarity, to detail retrieval and to outright fidelity, the PD5 is extremely hard to criticise and yes, it fully emphatically deserves a place in our best MP3 players guide. And its talents don’t stop there, not even close — its sound is punchily robust, effortlessly dynamic, brilliantly controlled and organised, and thoroughly engaging. If you take your portable listening experience seriously (or your desktop listening experience for that matter — the PD5 is also an excellent USB DAC), this Astell & Kern absolutely demands your attention. Away from audio quality the PD5 isn’t perfect; there are rare occasions on which it can be glitchy in operation, its on-screen menus are approaching ‘miniscule’, and it neither looks nor feels quite as expensive as it actually is. All of this, though, is made to seem fairly trivial by the way the PD5 performs its primary function. Astell & Kern PD5 review: Price and release date - Announced in August 2026; released in September 2026 The Astell & Kern PD5 digital audio player is on sale now, and in the United Kingdom it costs £899. In the United States it will set you back $1,049, while in Australia it goes for AU$1,349. Anyone familiar with such devices knows that for an A&K player, that's actually not so expensive — again, note my 'for an A&K player' wording there. This company's flagship DAPs go for $3,999 / £3,799 / AU$6,599 (Astell & Kern A&ultima SP4000 and its newer T-suffixed sibling, I'm looking at you), but you can also get a hi-res player from A&K's sub-brand — called the Activo P1 — for $430 / £399 (around AU$869). There are crucial differences in the specifications which I'll go into, but it's good to have an idea of the market at least, when looking at such a fee and being told by its makers that it is "entry level". - Eight (count ‘em!) Cirrus Logic CS43198 DACs - Balanced and unbalanced headphone outputs The PD5 isn’t the first Astell & Kern product that’s been so thoroughly specified that discussing every one of its features in any kind of depth might take up most of your day. So let’s say right from the off that no eventuality has been overlooked where the PD5 is concerned, and then let’s deal with the headlines and then try not to get too bogged down in all the rest of it… Never knowingly understated, Astell & Kern has fitted eight Cirrus Logic CS43198 DAC chipsets here. The user interface gives you the option of listening using four, or all eight — listening in octa-mode offers optimal sound quality, but eats into battery life quite badly (engage all eight DACs and you’re looking at 15 hours of playback as opposed to the 28 or so you should get when listening to ‘just’ four). Taking the battery from ‘flat’ to ‘full’ takes around two-and-a-half hours. In terms of feeding digital audio content to that considerable digital-to-analog conversion line-up, you have a few options. The bare-bones Android user interface Astell & Kern has deployed here, along with dual-band wi-fi, allows you to download the app of your favourite music streaming service(s), and 64GB of internal memory allows you to store some content to the PD5’s local storage. There’s a microSD card slot on the bottom of the frame (next to the USB-C slot that’s used for data transfer and for battery charging) too — it can accept cards of up to 1.5TB, which should prove adequate for all the hi-res content you might desire. The player can deal with resolutions of up to 32bit/384kHz PCM and DSD256, and is Roon Ready as well as featuring full-on Qobuz Connect integration. Or you might decide to bypass the fancy-pants D-to-A circuitry altogether and use Bluetooth to drive a pair of wireless headphones (although it does seem a bit of a weird idea to spend £899 on a player in order to use it like a smartphone). The PD5 features Bluetooth 5.3 with codec support up to and including aptX HD. It also has two headphone outputs: an unbalanced 3.5mm socket and a balanced 4.4mm alternative that’s compatible with five-pole jacks. Use the 4.4mm output, select octa-DAC mode, and the Astell & Kern can summon a mammoth 8Vrms of power — so even the most demanding headphones will have to do as they are told. But there are quite a few ways in which the sound can be affected, both by the device and by the person using it, before it reaches these outputs. The ‘EnviroTune’ feature uses a mic integrated into the top edge of the PD5 to analyse ambient noise in real time and correct those frequencies affected by it without just making everything louder. The ‘Teraton Alpha’ audio engine that’s familiar from some of Astell & Kern’s uber-pricey DAPs minimises noise from the power supply and creates amplification that’s as stable and distortion-free as possible. And ‘Enhanced Signal Alignment’ technology synchronises outgoing signals in an effort to negate phase distortion and deliver the most coherent sonic image possible. The end user, meanwhile, gets a choice of digital filters and some quite in-depth EQ adjustment to look into. The default filter is ‘low latency fast’, and it is as distinct in its effect as ‘low latency slow’, ‘phase compensated fast’ and ‘phase compensated slow’ are from each other. A ten-band EQ offers fairly granular adjustment of the sound, and an ‘advanced’ EQ interface allows frequency response to be defined using a graph with 20 (!) plotting points. The PD5 will function as a desktop too, thanks to its USB-C slot’s ability with data transfer. Simply make a hard connection to, say, your laptop, select ‘DAC input’ in the ‘USB Mode’ sub-menu, and the Astell & Kern automatically switches on octa-DAC mode in order to give your computer a proper go at sounding decent for once. - Clarity, detail and dynamism in equal measure The Astell & Kern PD5 is an admirably unpicky device, although obviously there are limits. Give it the sort of standard content available on a proper music streaming service (which means a CD-quality resolution of 16bit/44.1kHz) and it does an admirable job of maximising the information available to it. Step down from there, though, to the sort of squashed nonsense served up by Apple Music or Spotify, and the PD5 struggles to conceal its disdain. But you didn’t spend proper money to listen to compressed poverty-spec streams, did you? So a 16bit/44.1kHz stream of Hood’s Western Housing Concerns is delivered in tremendous fashion. The presentation is open and spacious, with an expansive soundstage on which each element of the recording gets ample room in which to stretch out and express itself. The layout is rigorously observed, and the PD5’s powers or organisation mean the stage is locked in place and completely convincing. Tonality is absolutely neutral, the player offering neither heat nor chill to the colour of the recording. There’s excellent clarity to the presentation, a really dark and quiet background in front of which the band perform — and at every stage of the frequency range, there’s absolutely fanatical attention to detail. No matter how minor an occurrence, how far back in the mix, or how fleeting, the Astell & Kern will seize upon it and give it precisely the amount of weight and emphasis it requires. Frequency response is similarly even-handed, and similarly convincing as a result. A switch to a DSD64 file of Michael Jackson’s Don’t Stop ‘Til You Get Enough reveals deep, textured, tremendously varied and thrillingly solid low-frequency response, and bass is controlled to the point that rhythmic expression is never less than positive and confident. Midrange resolution is no less accomplished, with the singer’s mic technique made every bit as apparent as his tone and timbre. The top of the frequency range strikes a lovely balance between substance and brilliance, and again there’s an absolutely stack of information available. The PD5 doesn’t over- or underemphasise any part of the frequency range, and as a result this glossy, audibly expensive recording sounds as natural and polished as it ever did. Dynamic headroom is considerable when it’s time to describe big variations in volume or intensity or attack, and the more subtle dynamics of harmonic variation and transient response are never overlooked. The entire presentation hangs together seamlessly, the Astell & Kern offering a proper sense of unity and singularity to recordings of every type. And perhaps best of all, there’s nothing show-y or even especially analytical about the way the PD5 goes about things. As far as insight into a recording goes it’s basically untouchable at the money, but that’s not what defines the Astell & Kern. It’s the energy of its sound, the engaged and engaging nature of its performance, that makes it as entertaining a listen as you’ll get from a portable device costing less than four figures. - 120 x 70 x 16mm (HxWxD) There’s absolutely nothing wrong with the Astell & Kern PD5 as a physical object, let me make that clear from the off. The dimensions are nicely palm-sized, the weight is sufficient to make it feel like a premium product without being a burden to a jacket pocket, and the standard of fit and finish is impeccable. And I’m not about to pretend I miss the painfully pointy edges of some previous Astell & Kern models, either — the PD5 is a much friendlier proposition in this respect — nor the painfully self-conscious offset screen of the old SR35. But there’s nothing remarkable about the design of the PD5, nothing to set it apart from the pack of products competing with it for your hard-earned. Even the volume dial, previously a little Astell & Kern design flourish, is unremarkable here. I realise I can’t have it all ways, and a calm and sensible aesthetic is preferable to something overwrought and wilful. But I find myself slightly concerned that for the PD5, Astell & Kern may have bypassed its industrial design team altogether… Astell & Kern PD5 review: Usability and setup As mentioned, the PD5 uses a stripped-back version of Android as its user interface — and it’s all the better for it. Too many digital audio players pointlessly include a lot of your smartphone’s functionality for no reason, as far as I can tell, other than to eat into the machine’s local memory. The 4.1in touchscreen is bright, although rather more reflective than is ideal, and it’s responsive without being on a hair trigger. The Astell & Kern’s menus are extensive, and as a result the font size is really very small — but squint and you should be able to make out what’s what (even if the occasional use of ‘red on black’ for text is a terrible idea). Setting up the PD5 to your satisfaction isn’t the work of a moment. But when you finally get finished you can at least be sure you have a digital audio player that’s primed to do exactly what you want, and in the manner you want it. There are occasional glitches in operation, though — or, at least, that’s my experience. I install the Tidal music streaming app, and also insert a microSD card full of hi-res content. But every now and then, both sources will play at the same time. Pressing ‘play’ on a Tidal file usually stops playback from the local storage and vice versa — but not always, which is a weird one and no mistake. Because the majority of the money you’ve spent on a PD5 has gone on the internals, it’s difficult to suggest its perceived value is especially high even if you accept that it’s beautifully constructed and even quite tactile. No, the value for money Astell & Kern is offering here doesn’t reveal itself until you start listening — and then it becomes quickly apparent that your money has been very well spent indeed. Should I buy the Astell & Kern PD5? Buy it if... The PD5 is equipped to make even the most difficult headphones bend to its will. You’re after uncompromised sound quality With the Astell & Kern you get what you pay for and then some. You’re sharp-eyed as well as sharp-eared Navigating those set-up menus is no job for anyone who’s misplaced their spectacles. Don't buy it if... You want to see, as well as hear, where your money has gone The PD5 is a perfectly pleasant little device, but its appearance doesn’t exactly shout “almost a grand!” The Astell & Kern sounds perfectly fine via Bluetooth, but really your smartphone will do a pretty similar job. The FiiO M23 has been around for a couple of years now, but really this only means it’s now competing almost directly with the PD5 on price. It remains a biggish, bulky-ish device, it’s true, but it also remains one of the most poised, direct and downright musical digital audio players around. Give it the right stuff to work with in terms of content and headphones, and the sound quality is enthralling. Read our full FiiO M23 review - Popped a 512GB microSD card loaded with extremely hi-res content into it - Used Sennheiser IE900 and Meze Audio Strada for most of my testing Then I connected a pair of Sennheiser IE900 IEMs using the 4.4mm balanced output, and also used a pair of Meze Audio Strada headphones connected the same way. I also investigated the PD5’s desktop DAC credentials by plugging it into an Apple MacBook Pro and using the Qobuz and Tidal desktop apps to listen to hi-res using the same pairs of headphones.
