item.title: REVIEW: Sonos Ace Ultra Review: A Classy Rival to Sony and Bose Headphones
item.description:
Source: PCMag
I really like Sonos' first headphones, the Ace, which were released in 2024. They have a sleek, stylish design, sound pretty good, and have at least some Sonos integration, even if it's a little lacking. The $449 Ace Ultra is the company's do-over, with sonic upgrades and a new feature called Headphone Linking, which transfers audio between the headphones and compatible Sonos speakers over Wi-Fi. The new model lands in a fiercely competitive field alongside the $449 Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) and the $459.99 Sony WH-1000XM6. Although the Ace Ultra doesn't quite have the ANC and feature set to make it the default recommendation at this price point—that still goes to Sony's XM6, our Editors' Choice—it does have ANC that's almost as good, an excellent audio response, and deep Sonos integration. I'm happy to see that the Ace Ultra follows the design language of the original Ace pretty closely. It's a clean, modern-looking pair of over-ear headphones with a reinforced headband and plush rebound-foam cushions on the earcups. It comes in four matte finishes—Black and Soft White are widely available, while Agave and Sand are sold through Sonos and select retailers. The ear cushions are replaceable, and Sonos says the battery is too, though the company notes battery replacement is "intended for a skilled operator" rather than a casual user swap. At 11.3 ounces (322 grams), the Ace Ultra isn't unusually heavy for an over-ear headphone, though it's not particularly light either. It weighs more than the QuietComfort Ultra and XM6, but less than the AirPods Max 2 ($549). That said, I find them to be quite comfortable. The headband does a great job at distributing weight across the top of the head, and while the earcups can get slightly warm in warmer weather, that's fairly common. For controls, the left earcup has a power button, while the right earcup has a noise-control button that activates your voice assistant when held down. It also has what Sonos calls the Content Key, which handles volume, playback, calls, and transfer for Headphone Linking. It's a tactile slider for easy volume control, which I like. Plus, it means you don't have to search for lots of different buttons to control separate media and playback functions. That said, the physical controls aren't customizable beyond selecting which noise modes are cycled through (ANC and Aware Mode by default, with Off available if you enable it in the app), turning wear detection on or off, and a handful of app toggles like Sidetone and Wear to Answer. The headphones connect over Bluetooth 6.0 for standard device streaming and Wi-Fi for Sonos system linking at home. There's a USB-C port for digital audio and charging, plus a bundled USB-C-to-3.5mm cable for analog sources like airplane entertainment systems. Codec support includes lossless audio through USB-C, along with AAC, SBC, aptX Lossless, and aptX Adaptive over Bluetooth. Lossless over Bluetooth requires a Snapdragon Sound-enabled Android device; recent Motorola phones like the Razr Fold support it, but none from Samsung do. The Arc Ultra headphones also have Bluetooth Multipoint for simultaneous connectivity with two devices. Each ear cup houses a new custom 40mm driver with what Sonos describes as a revised motor structure and an additional outer-ring magnet. The company claims deeper bass, more detail, and lower distortion than the original Ace's drivers. Battery life is upgraded, too. The headphones get up to an impressive 35 hours with ANC on, which beats the XM6, QuietComfort Ultra, AirPods Max 2, and the original Sonos Ace headphones, which offered 30 hours with ANC. When they do run out of juice, three minutes of charging gets three hours of playback, and a full charge takes around three hours. The headphones come with a USB-C cable, a USB-C-to-3.5mm cable, and a carry case with a removable cable pouch. Sonos says the case uses roughly 80% recycled content, which is always nice to see. I really like how slim and sleek the case is, though I did find that the zip regularly got caught when I was trying to open or close it. The Sonos app has gotten quite a bit better since the company rolled out a controversial new design back in 2024. Through the app, you'll be able to customize many of the controls and features, including switching noise modes. Headphone Linking is one of the more interesting features here. If you have a compatible Sonos speaker or soundbar, Wi-Fi, and the Sonos app, it pulls audio from the nearest speaker when you press and hold the Content Key, then another press-and-hold sends it back the same way. Note that the feature is still in beta, and Sonos bills it "as is," so you might experience some bugs. That said, it is still a fair bit more advanced than the soundbar-only feature that was available on the original Sonos Ace headphones. The feature worked pretty well in my testing. It judges the "closest" speaker based on Wi-Fi signal, and it did a pretty good job at that, though if you have Sonos speakers around the house, like I do, you'll find that the "closest" speaker isn't always the one in the room you're in. Still, it worked well enough. The EQ is expanded, too. In fact, there are two equalizers. The default is a three-band EQ with sliders for bass, mid, and treble, but there's also an Advanced mode that gives you a full eight-band EQ, with bands ranging from 46Hz to 10kHz. That makes it much easier to customize the headphones' tuning for those who want to. Sonos claims the Ace Ultra delivers "up to 2x more" noise cancellation than the original Ace, powered by adaptive processing and the expanded 10-microphone array, with the comparison specified at low frequencies up to 65Hz. The headphones support Adaptive ANC too, helping to ensure they remain usable if you change the fit or the noise in your environment changes. In testing, I'm not sure if the ANC is really twice as good, but it's certainly better than the original Sonos Ace headphones. When it comes to things like plane noise, the headphones did a very good job of cutting out the vast majority of engine noise, leaving only some background white noise that was very easy to cover up with any audio playing. They weren't as impressive on a city bus, but still performed very well, letting through only some inconsistent noise from things like doors opening and closing, and creaking sounds from the suspension. In a cafe, the headphones cut out the vast majority of background chatter, and while it was possible to hear nearby voices, those voices were dramatically quieter. That's all to say the headphones are very near the best of the best when it comes to ANC, but not quite on par. The AirPods Max 2, Sony WH-1000XM6, and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) are slightly better when it comes to ANC, but not so much that you'd be missing out on a lot by going for these headphones instead. The Aware Mode built into the headphones isn't the best, but it's not terrible. It can sound slightly amplified in certain environments, but it does a pretty good job of faithfully reproducing the full frequency range, including the high frequencies that headphones often miss. It's not, however, as impressive as the AirPods Max, which sound more natural and don't hiss as much as the Sonos headphones do with Aware Mode active. Sonos says the Ace Ultra's new 40mm drivers were tuned with input from Grammy- and Oscar-winning engineers and feature a revised motor structure with an additional outer-ring magnet. The idea is that the headphones deliver richer low end, clearer detail, and lower distortion—and ultimately, I did find them to sound great. Much of the improvements came from better bass response. The bass was smooth, deep, and powerful, thankfully without getting muddy or overbearing. On a track like "Silent Shout" by The Knife, the sub-bass content was largely well-delivered, complementing the rest of the mix. That was coupled with crisp-sounding highs and a nice, wide soundstage. The track sounded very warm, but certainly not in a bad way. On "Loyalty" by Kendrick Lamar, the bass was on show even more, and again, it delivered. The headphones reproduced all but the deepest sub-bass notes on the track and weren't overpowering or too heavy, though they erred on the side of bass-heavy rather than neutral. The vocals from Lamar and Rihanna were warm and clear, while the track's percussion was reasonably crisp. The Sonos Ace Ultra headphones sounded great on more natural-sounding tracks like "Drover" by Bill Callahan, though I found the track sounded a little warmer than I would have liked. Callahan's deep vocal was quite resonant and felt a little too low-mid-heavy at times. That said, the acoustic guitar was nice and crisp, offering a good sense of rhythm throughout the track, while the cymbals and other percussion had good sizzle. On orchestral tracks, like the opening scene to The Gospel According to the Other Mary by John Adams, the wide soundstage helped ensure there was plenty of room for all the different sections. The lower strings were definitely emphasized on this track, but the higher strings still had a nice timbre, while the brass instruments sounded bright enough. The solo vocalist nicely cut through the middle of the mix, too. Overall, the headphones could be described as warm and somewhat bass-heavy. They're not neutral, but that's not necessarily a bad thing unless you're explicitly looking for neutral headphones. I do prefer a slightly toned-down low-mid response, but thanks to the new EQ, I was able to get that pretty easily. The built-in microphones are fine for call quality. My voice was a little muffled, but I was still able to understand the words I spoke perfectly fine. It’s not the best-sounding call quality out there, but you won’t have issues with people understanding you. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Sonos Ace Ultra headphones are a definite upgrade over the original Ace. They sound better, integrate more seamlessly with other Sonos speakers, and deliver improved ANC and battery life. The Sony WH-1000XM6 remains a better buy for most, with still-better ANC and sound quality, but Sonos beats them in endurance. Meanwhile, the AirPods Max 2 can transfer audio between devices like an Apple TV and any AirPlay-compatible speakers, including Sonos speakers, though it uses the AirPlay UI on a device rather than a simple button press. Still, if you're deep in the Sonos ecosystem, the Ace Ultra headphones have a lot to offer. They're attractive, well-designed, and above all, sound superb. Christian de Looper is a freelance consumer tech reporter based in sunny Santa Cruz, California. With a Bachelor's Degree in Music Technology, Christian leverages his industry knowledge to review audio products for PCMag, including Bluetooth headphones and speakers. He also contributes to Tom’s Guide, Digital Trends, Mashable, ZDNet, and others, where he reviews audio, mobile, smart home, and computing gear.

item.title: REVIEW: EasySMX S10 Lite review: A Switch 2 fidget toy with a weird removable faceplate
item.description:
Source: Engadget
EasySMX S10 Lite review: A Switch 2 fidget toy with a weird removable faceplate EasySMX is using Elizabeth Holmes levels of pedantry with this faceplate situation. Of all the Switch 2 controllers I've reviewed in 2026, this is probably the most unexpected pick. EasySMX isn't as well-known as 8BitDo or Turtle Beach, and the S10 Lite is its most pared-down Switch 2 gamepad, regularly listed for $40. The price is exactly what intrigued me about the S10 Lite in the first place, considering most Switch 2 controllers cost around $70, and Nintendo's own Pro Controller is $90. A feature-rich gamepad that can potentially compete with 8BitDo's incredible, $30 Ultimate 2C? I'm here for it. And then just as swiftly, I'm gone. While the EasySMX S10 Lite has supremely tactile buttons, Hall effect sticks with a soft-hit feel, motion controls and strong haptics, it also has a semi-transparent, magnetically attached faceplate that's so wonky and cheap-feeling that it overshadows the controller's more attractive features. I'm someone who tends to enjoy oddball ideas in my gaming accessories and I can't fully make sense of the S10 Lite faceplate. The way that EasySMX has chosen to market this removable piece of plastic, using misleading verbiage around the availability of custom options, has only poured fuel on the confusion fire. First, the basics and the good bits. The EasySMX S10 Lite is indeed light and compact, with a creamy plastic finish along the body and an anti-slip diamond texture on the backs of the grips. There are two buttons on the rear of the controller, mappable by pressing and holding a small nearby input marked M. I wish the rear buttons crept up the sides of the grips more, allowing my fingertips to more comfortably hit them, but they're certainly within reach and nice to have. The S10 Lite comes in two colors, ice blue or pastel pink, and while the pink is clearly the cuter option, they're both charming. There are some fabulous modern features built into the S10 Lite, including precise, anti-drift Hall effect analog sticks that hit the sides of their enclosures silently and super softly. The sound and feel is comparable to Nintendo's proprietary soft-hit action on the Pro Controller, which is a notable feat. That said, the stick click on the S10 Lite is a little too stiff for my liking, and it does make an audible pop when pressed. I'm not personally complaining about the noise, which I find soothing on an ASMR level, but it's notable when the sticks themselves are so darn pillowy otherwise. The face buttons are tactile microswitches with a wonderfully clicky sound and feel. However, they're also fairly rigid, especially compared with something like the springy mechanical buttons on Razer's Wolverine V3 Pro (my personal favorite gamepad, though it only supports PC and Xbox, and also costs an eye-watering $200. See? I told you the price point was appealing here). The haptics in the S10 Lite are nice and strong, with four intensity settings, and at most they make a slight whining sound rather than grinding. The bumpers and wide-flared triggers stand out prominently from the chassis, and the triggers have a clicky microswitch action like the face buttons. While I do adore fidget-toy features in my controllers — and the S10 Lite definitely delivers on this point — in-game, I prefer a smooth and sensitive Hall effect pull in the triggers. It's a tradeoff between satisfying sounds and modern comfort that you'll have to consider for yourself. I like that the home, GameChat and capture buttons are lined up at the bottom of the controller's face, separate from the plus and minus inputs in the center of the pad. This configuration should reduce the number of random, accidental screenshots that you end up taking while trying to quickly open the inventory in Resident Evil Requiem or peep the menu in Hello Kitty Island Adventure, for completely random example. The S10 Lite has nine-axis motion controls and a Turbo function that allows you to set input macros to a simple button combo. It's also able to wake up the Switch 2 from afar, one of the raddest features a controller can have. The quick-start card that's included in the box is actually helpful in terms of connecting the gamepad to the console. And what's more, there's a built-in toggle on the backside of the pad that lets you swap between Switch and Switch 2 compatibility, or PC, Android and iOS play. In the box, you get the gamepad, a charging cable and the instruction card. The gamepad, of course, includes the faceplate, attached with four visible, circular magnets and some tension. When I pulled my S10 Lite out of the box, the bottom ridge of the faceplate wasn't fully tucked into place, raised in a way that was mildly infuriating but not clearly unintentional. It wasn't until I was fidgeting with the controller, waiting for a game to download, that I realized I could pop in the transparent-blue plastic so it sat flat along the bottom. Even still, the left side of my faceplate refuses to depress as deeply as the right, so there's a sliver of icy plastic peering over one grip, catching my fingertips and compelling me to pick at it. I may be able to adjust this by tightening a tiny screw on that side, but all things considered, I'd rather not have to. This leads us to the obvious question: Why have a removable faceplate in the first place? It would make sense if EasySMX had, say, a marketplace of cute alternatives that anyone could purchase and swap into their own pad, allowing the brand to jump on trends and collaborate with cool creators, naturally extending the money-making potential of the S10 Lite. That would make perfect sense. But that's not what EasySMX is doing. The controller's product page provides just one sentence about faceplates, reading, "DIY Your Controller: express your personality with DIY Magnetic Faceplates & Stickers, allowing you to swap covers instantly to match your mood or your favorite game theme." Those first three letters are doing the heavy lifting, since EasySMX doesn't actually sell replacement or custom faceplates of any kind. The only way to guarantee you'll get one is to make it yourself, but even then, it appears that 3D files and high-quality images of the faceplates aren't publicly available. The company also doesn't sell stickers, an additional accessory it mentions without prompting. With this context in mind, it's unclear what EasySMX means by DIY Your Controller, but it feels like a purposefully misleading, weaselly turn of phrase — like Elizabeth Holmes saying to Nathan Fielder, "You can see everything." EasySMX does hold giveaways for customized faceplates on Reddit and Discord every now and then, it seems, but these are scattered. It's possible that the company is gathering data and ramping up to produce faceplates that players can buy, but right now, they're weirdly unattainable. I really like tactile buttons, soft-hit sticks and the idea of modular art on my controller, but I really, really hate being lied to, and it kinda feels like that's what EasySMX is doing with the faceplate situation. The EasySMX S10 Lite is fine for kids (or adults) who love a good click and don't mind a messy faceplate, but otherwise, this thing is never beating the 8BitDo Ultimate 2C in terms of affordability and features.

item.title: REVIEW: REDMAGIC Astra 2 review: I finally found a no-holds-barred warrior for tablet gaming
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
“An unapologetically over-the-top slate that also delivers.”
I have a weakness for small tablets, and this love started years ago with the iPad mini. Unfortunately, with each passing year, most brands push their slates closer to laptop territory, with 12-inch, 13-inch, and even 14-inch screens that need a keyboard and a desk to make sense. The REDMAGIC Astra 2 goes the other way. It’s a 9.06-inch tablet built for one job above all else, which is gaming in your hands, and it does that job better than any Android tablet I’ve used. The hardware is pretty generous. You get Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, up to 16GB of LPDDR5T RAM, and an active liquid cooling system that replaces the tiny fan from the first Astra. The result is performance that holds steady long after other Android flagships start to throttle. The 2.4K OLED screen runs at up to 185Hz, and hits 1,600 nits at peak brightness. REDMAGIC also got the small things right. The camera sits completely flush, and there are two USB-C ports for charging in either orientation with a bypass trick. It’s not a tablet for everyone, though. The price has jumped to $799 for the heavy-hitter model, the software ships with a pile of third-party apps, the cameras are weak, and REDMAGIC’s update promise is short outside Europe. The Astra 2 is a specialist machine, and it doesn’t pretend to be an iPad replacement. But if raw gaming firepower is what you seek, this is where your search ends. REDMAGIC Astra 2 specifications: A quick look at the internal hardware REDMAGIC Astra 2 design and build: Bold is all I can say about it The REDMAGIC Astra 2 measures 207.1 x 134.2 x 6.9mm and weighs 363 grams, roughly 7 grams less than its predecessor. That may not sound like much on paper, but the overall footprint is what matters here. This is a tablet I can hold in one hand, or cradle with two for a long gaming session, without my forearms complaining. Broadly, you won’t be forced to rest this one on your lap or prop it on a table. The 16:10 aspect ratio helps, too. In landscape, there’s enough width for your thumbs and for widescreen video. In portrait, the tablet doesn’t feel top-heavy when I’m reading a web page, a PDF, or a manga chapter. It is noticeably heavier than Apple’s iPad mini, mostly due to the cooling hardware inside, but the weight is evenly spread, and the 6.9mm profile gives it a dense, solid feel rather than a hollow one. RedMagic uses an aviation-grade aluminum frame and back, available in Eclipse (black) and Starfrost (silver) shades. The matte, blasted finish offers far more grip than the glossy glass backs on the company’s gaming phones, and I never had to worry about it sliding off a sofa armrest. My favorite design detail is on the back: there’s no camera bump. The single 13-megapixel sensor sits completely flush under the glass, so the tablet lies flat on a desk or a tray table without rocking. It’s a small detail, but almost every phone and tablet I test these days wobbles when you tap it on a table, and the Astra 2 doesn’t. On the front, the bezels are slim and even, giving the tablet a 90.1% screen-to-body ratio. REDMAGIC also avoided punching a camera hole into the display. The 9MP selfie camera lives in the bezel, so nothing interrupts a movie, an e-book, or the corner of a game’s HUD where your minimap usually sits. Overall, the Astra 2 is far more restrained than REDMAGIC’s phones, but the back still makes its gaming roots clear. A transparent glass window shows off a stylized circuit board design and the tablet’s headline feature: an active liquid cooling loop. Instead of a sealed copper heat pipe or a vapor chamber alone, the Astra 2 circulates a non-conductive, server-grade fluorinated coolant across its internal heat spreaders. When the tablet is under load, you can actually see the coolant moving behind the window, lit by programmable RGB lighting. You can set it to a solid color, such as an electric blue or green, or switch it off entirely if you plan to use the tablet in a meeting and would rather not draw attention. REDMAGIC placed every port and button with landscape gaming in mind, and for the most part, it shows. The tablet has two USB-C ports. The main one, on the short edge, supports USB 3.2 Gen 2 speeds of up to 10Gbps, DisplayPort Alt Mode for external monitors and AR glasses, and 75W charging. The second port, in the middle of the long bottom edge, runs at USB 2.0 speeds but also supports full 75W charging. In practice, that means I can plug in a charger while gaming without a cable digging into my palm, which is something I wish more tablets would copy. Along the upper right edge sits REDMAGIC’s signature red slider. Flick it, and the tablet jumps straight from the regular Android launcher into Game Space, REDMAGIC’s console-style gaming environment. If you don’t care about that, you can remap the switch to toggle the flashlight, start the voice recorder, or change sound profiles. The power button doubles as a fingerprint sensor, and it’s fast and reliable. Its position is a little odd, though. In landscape, it falls naturally under my left index finger, but in portrait, I have to reach up toward the top of the frame. Face unlock works well enough as a backup that I used it most of the time. The speakers are where the design falls short. REDMAGIC tuned the stereo pair with DTS:X Ultra, but the grilles sit low on the short edges. When I hold the tablet horizontally with both hands, my palms end up partially covering them, and the sound gets muffled. I had to angle my grip forward or switch to earbuds for longer sessions. The front glass is Corning Gorilla Glass 3. It holds up well against scratches, but it’s an old formulation, and I’d expect Victus or something newer at this price. The Astra 2 is IP54-rated. Dropping the fan from the previous model also means there are no open intake vents for dust and grit to work their way inside. Still, IP54 only covers light dust and splashes, so keep it away from the pool. The retail box is spartan. There’s no case and no screen protector, and in Western and European markets, there’s no charger either, just a red USB-C cable and some paperwork. Since the tablet has no built-in kickstand, you’ll also want to budget for a folio or stand if you plan to watch anything on a desk. The 9.06-inch OLED panel has a resolution of 2,400 x 1,504 pixels, which works out to 313 pixels per inch. The 16:10 shape is, in my opinion, the right choice for a tablet like this. Tall 20:9 phone screens feel cramped for reading and maps, while the 4:3 screens on most tablets leave thick black bars above and below widescreen video. On the Astra 2, movies and shows fill nearly the entire screen with very little letterboxing. As you turn it to portrait mode, you get a comfortable, book-like page for e-books, manuals, and social feeds. The refresh rate goes all the way up to 185Hz. I’ll be honest here, though. In everyday use, I struggled to tell the difference between 120Hz and 185Hz. But scrolling through menus, long web pages, and supported games is consistently smooth, and nothing ever felt choppy. REDMAGIC pairs the fast panel with a dedicated Synaptics display chip that drives a 300Hz multi-finger touch reporting rate and an instant touch sampling rate of up to 2,000Hz. In fast competitive shooters, the gap between touching the screen and seeing my character react felt practically nonexistent. If you’re coming from a 60Hz or 120Hz tablet, you’ll notice the difference right away. Being an OLED panel, the Astra 2 shows true blacks by switching individual pixels off completely. Bright highlights stand out against dark scenes without the blooming or the grayish haze I see on the LCD screens of many competing tablets. The panel covers 100% of the DCI-P3 color space, and REDMAGIC claims a Delta E below 1. Those are excellent numbers for a gaming-focused device. REDMAGIC doesn’t make much noise about HDR on the box, but the tablet supports HDR10+ and Dolby Vision playback. The screen is pretty bright. In fact, it’s comfortably one of the brightest compact Android tablets I’ve tested, and I had no trouble reading it near a sunny window or in a bright meeting room. Combined with SGS low-blue-light certification and flicker-free dimming, the panel makes late-night reading in a dark room fairly easy on the eyes. Raw performance is what the REDMAGIC Astra 2 is all about, and it doesn’t disappoint. Powering this slate is Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, built on a 3nm process. It has two prime Oryon Gen 3 cores clocked at 4.60GHz and six performance cores humming at 3.63GHz. Graphics are handled by the Adreno 840 GPU ticking at 1.2GHz, and REDMAGIC adds its own RedCore R4 chip, which takes care of audio, haptics, and lighting so the main processor can focus on games. You can choose between 12GB or 16GB of LPDDR5TXRAM and 256GB or 512GB of UFS 4.1 storage. REDMAGIC has dropped the 24GB RAM and 1TB storage options from the previous generation to keep costs in check, and there’s no microSD slot, either. The storage is fast, though. In my testing, sequential read pace consistently hit over 1,500 MB/s and sequential write speeds touched 1,600 MB/s. The numbers make it clear that this is the most powerful Android tablet you can buy right now. Coming to synthetic benchmarks, on Geekbench 6, the Astra 2 averaged 3,600+ in single-core and 11,600+ in multi-core runs. Single-core results are in the same league as Apple’s M4 silicon, which is no mean feat, while falling only about 6-8% shy on multi-core tests. AnTuTu v11 returned 4,285,000 points on average after three runs, which is, once again, quite impressive. On 3DMark Wild Life Unlimited, it managed to comfortably stay ahead of other 8.8-inch gaming tablets. The ray-tracing-focused Solar Bay Extreme test returned expectedly high scores, but the more impressive aspect was the low perf drop from peak value and high stability. This is where the Astra 2 sets itself apart. Most tablets lose performance over time as heat builds up inside a sealed body. REDMAGIC has replaced the 20,000 RPM fan from the last generation with the AquaCore 2.0 system, which combines liquid metal thermal paste on the chip, a large 3D vapor chamber, and the circulating coolant liquid in a loop. In a continuous 20-minute stress test, the Astra 2 held between 82% and 95% of its peak performance. Most tablets in the flagship bracket often drop to 60-65% under the same load. The aluminum shell does get warm. My infrared thermometer read between 97°F and 100°F after long gaming and video sessions, but the chip itself didn’t throttle in any way I could notice. It’s far quieter than the whirring fan on the original Astra. The 185Hz screen is the Astra 2’s headline feature, but very few games can actually take advantage of it. I ran more than a dozen titles with the display set to 185Hz, and a boosted performance profile enabled. I left Diablo mode off for most of my testing, since REDMAGIC designed it to be used with an external clip-on cooler. Only one game ran at a true 185 fps in my tests. Most of the marquee titles topped out at 120 fps, a few landed well below that, and a couple ran into odd problems. Blood Strike is the game that shows off what this tablet can do. With graphics settings maxed out, it held a steady 185 fps, and it’s the first time I’ve seen a mobile shooter run at such a high frame rate. It was also the only game that pushed the battery temperature close to 110 degrees Fahrenheit, the highest reading I saw, with the exception of Diablo mode. Call of Duty: Mobile comes close. In multiplayer, the frame counter was consistently over 160 fps, but only once I dropped the graphics to lower quality. With everything maxed out, it settles at around 60 fps, which still looks fantastic on this screen. Battle Royale is more demanding, but I was glad to see 90+ fps on this one as well. I can also report that the gyroscope aiming worked well across the full slate of games I tried. PUBG’s local fork also ran at a smooth 120 fps on its peak frame rate setting. The motion was so fluid that it actually left me a little dizzy after a long session. Delta Force also held 120 fps without any trouble. Farlight 84 hit 119 to 120 fps, but not at its highest settings. Turning the graphics up drops the cap to 90 fps, and the ultra preset limits you to 60 fps. Fortnite, with every setting on Epic and the 120 fps option enabled, hovered between 90 and 94 fps. Dropping the texture quality a notch should get you closer to 120 fps, though. Wuthering Waves, one of the most demanding games out there, deserves a note. On its peak preset, the game caps out at 90 fps. With REDMAGIC’s frame interpolation enabled, it easily climbed past 100 fps, and I didn’t run into any vexing stutters while at it. The REDMAGIC Astra 2’s biggest undoing is the gaming ecosystem, because the hardware is more than ready for whatever you throw at it. Genshin Impact, for example, was a letdown. With graphics maxed out, it ran at only around 45 fps, below the game’s own 60 fps cap, and turning on frame interpolation made no visible difference. Asphalt Legends Unite offers a 120 fps option, but in practice, it ran barely above 50 fps. Minecraft was the worst of the bunch. It mostly held 60 fps, but I ran into noticeable freezes in the middle of play. Dropping the performance mode to Balanced or Eco and setting the screen to 60Hz is worth trying, but I can’t promise it fixes the problem. This looks like a compatibility issue that REDMAGIC or the game’s developers will need to address. Overall, the frame interpolation tech feels unfinished, and it’s nowhere close to what the likes of Nvidia’s DLSS or AMD’s FSR will provide. It worked in Wuthering Waves, remained static in Genshin Impact, and wasn’t even available in Call of Duty: Mobile or Delta Force. I hope REDMAGIC improves the situation with updates. The liquid cooling does its job, and better than I expected. In a room at around 82.4°F, the battery temperature stayed between 100.4°F and 104.0°F in most games, and only Blood Strike at 185 fps pushed it to 110°F. I never saw the tablet slow down because of heat, even after hours of back-to-back sessions. Diablo mode is a different story. When I pushed Fortnite to its absolute limit, with its 120 fps mode enabled, the game ran smoothly, but the temperature climbed all the way to 127°F. Yes, the tablet got pretty warm. Once I closed the game, though, the liquid cooling system brought the temperature down to 110°F in roughly three minutes, and within six minutes, it had dropped below 102°F. The liquid cooling system works well beyond games, as well. After running a synthetic benchmark test, the battery and board sensors had soared to 104°F and 111°F, respectively. Five minutes later, the numbers had dropped to 91°F and 93°F for the battery and board, respectively. The speed of cooling came as a pleasant surprise to me. The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 also makes the Astra 2 one of the most capable Android devices for running PC games through compatibility layers like GameHub. Older titles such as Halo run at over 60 fps, and even Marvel’s Spider-Man: Miles Morales is playable at 60fps on low graphics settings with upscaling and frame generation enabled. Demanding games like The Witcher 3 and Crysis Remastered also run well, but you’ll need to drop the resolution and juice up frame generation. Compatibility is still hit-or-miss, though, and online multiplayer PC games usually get blocked by anti-cheat software. It’s a fun bonus rather than a reason to buy the tablet. As you flick the red switch, Game Space takes over the screen with a console-style launcher environment for games and plenty of customization options. Your games appear in a carousel, and you can adjust graphics, controls, and performance for each one. Swiping in from the corners during a game brings up the Energy Cube overlay, which is where most of the useful controls live. There are four performance profiles. Eco for saving battery, Balanced for everyday play, Rise for unlocked CPU and GPU clocks, and Diablo, which goes all out and is designed for use with an external clip-on cooler. A feature called Super Picture Quality uses on-device AI to upscale games and interpolate the frames for higher fps output. You can also turn off Android’s edge gestures so a stray swipe doesn’t throw you out of a game mid-fight. Beyond that, there are tactical plugins such as on-screen crosshairs, color filters that make enemies easier to spot in dark areas, and an optional AI coach. Some of them feel like cheat codes, and they will almost certainly get you banned from competitive tournaments. Console Mode lets you send a 4K gaming interface to a TV or monitor over USB-C, which turns the Astra 2 into a decent living room setup. REDMAGIC Astra 2 Software: Loaded and bloated The Astra 2 runs REDMAGIC OS 11.5 on top of Android 16. It’s a heavy re-skinning, mind you! REDMAGIC’s software has been its strength (thanks to all those plug-ins and customizations) and a crucial weakness, with flashy styling, buggy launchers, and awkwardly translated menus. I’m happy to report that this version is much cleaner, though not a full salvation. Out of the box, the interface sticks close to Google’s Material You design, with a standard app drawer, round icons, and settings menus where you’d expect them. REDMAGIC has also finally added Google Discover to the left of the home screen, which was missing on its earlier devices. If you still want the cyberpunk look, gaudy themes and fonts are just a toggle away. As a gaming and entertainment device, the Astra 2 is superb. As a work machine, it’s limited. Split-screen and floating windows are both there, so I could watch a video while replying to messages or keep notes open next to a browser. But the 9-inch screen doesn’t have enough room for two full productivity apps side by side. REDMAGIC also lacks a native desktop mode like Samsung DeX or OnePlus Open Canvas, so the Astra 2 stays firmly in phone app territory rather than working as a laptop stand-in. The setup process is a tad annoying. The setup wizard tries to preselect around a dozen third-party apps and casual games for download, and I had to uncheck them one by one. Even after that, the tablet ships with a few pre-installed apps, along with a handful of casual games. There are also a few duplicate system utilities, some of which can’t be purged. I cleaned most of it up in under an hour, but it shouldn’t be my job in the first place, and it somewhat dilutes an otherwise stellar experience of all using an all-out tablet. The biggest weakness of the Astra 2 is how long it will be supported. Apple, Google, and Samsung now offer six to seven years of OS upgrades and security patches. REDMAGIC’s policy depends on where you live. Buyers in the European Union get up to five years of support, thanks to regional regulations. Everywhere else, including North America, REDMAGIC promises just two major Android upgrades and three years of security updates. For a tablet that costs as much, it’s a major problem if you expect to use it for several years. REDMAGIC Astra 2 battery and charging: Fast, with an unexpected perk The REDMAGIC Astra 2 comes equipped with an 8,300mAh battery, a small step up from the original Astra. Despite the powerful chip and high-refresh screen, the uptake is fairly frugal in everyday use. In my web browsing-based work disguised as a test, the tablet lasted around 8-9 hours, which is more than enough for a full day of usage. If you binge-watch a TV series or films, it can easily go around 9 hours. Thankfully, standby battery drain is low. I left the tablet idle on my desk for a week, and it used less than 30% of its battery. Of course, heavy games drain the battery much faster. Starting at 99%, I played demanding titles back to back for about three hours with the screen at 185Hz and ended at 31%. That works out to roughly 25% for nearly every hour, or about 4-4.5 hours of heavy gaming on a full charge. If you switch to Diablo mode, it will cut those per-charge numbers further down and lead to heating, as well. That’s a big drop compared with browsing, but it’s still roughly double what you’d get from handhelds like the Steam Deck or Asus ROG Ally. Lighter casual games can stretch runtime much further. Charging is fast, thankfully, and without the usual heating caveat. With a USB-C Power Delivery brick that supports the tablet’s 75W protocol, the Astra 2 went from empty to 67% in 30 minutes, and reached a full tank in 55 minutes. Both USB-C ports support the full 75W top-up, so you can run the cable out of whichever edge suits your grip. REDMAGIC also includes Charge Separation tech on this tablet. With this feature enabled, power from the adapter goes straight to the processor and skips the battery entirely. That cuts down on the heat generated by charging while gaming, and in turn, helps preserve battery health over long sessions. If you game while plugged in, this is the mode you want to pick. Should you buy? If you’re buying a tablet mainly for games, the answer is a resounding yes. The REDMAGIC Astra 2 is the best Android gaming tablet I’ve used, and it proves that liquid cooling in a compact 9-inch body is more than just a gimmick. The combination of Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip, a 185Hz 2.4K OLED screen, a flat back, and dual fast-charging ports makes it a fantastic portable machine for mobile gamers, emulation fans, and anyone who simply wants the fastest small tablet around. Its sustained performance, bright screen, and bypass charging give it an edge that bigger mainstream tablets can’t match. It’s a much harder sell for everyone else. At $699, it competes directly with heavy-hitting tablets that do far more outside of games. On top of it, the preinstalled clutter, the easily muffled speakers, the lack of stylus and cellular support, and the short update promise outside Europe make it a tough recommendation as a digital sketchbook or even a daily productivity companion. In a nutshell, if gaming, emulation, and watching video on a gorgeous compact OLED screen are your priorities, buy the Astra 2 without second thoughts. If you need long-term software support, stylus input, or real productivity apps, your money will take you further elsewhere. Apple iPad mini (2026) The iPad mini remains the benchmark for small tablets, and the new model narrows the gap with an OLED screen and the A20 Pro chip. It doesn’t have the Astra 2’s high refresh rate or active cooling, so it won’t hold peak performance as long under heavy loads. In return, you get a more polished build, Apple Pencil support, iPadOS apps that are actually designed for tablets, and many more years of software updates. Just be aware that the most powerful version of its chip is reserved for the pricier storage tiers. Lenovo Legion Tab (Gen 5) This one is the Astra 2’s most direct Android rival, and owing to the high demand, it’s usually out of stock. This sleek slate offers a similar compact, gaming-first design, snappy performance, and dual USB-C ports for a little less money. If you want a dedicated Android gaming tablet but can’t justify REDMAGIC’s price, the Legion Tab is the one I’d look at first. iPad Air (M4) In case you prefer to spend your money on a do-everything tablet, the iPad Air is the safer choice. The Apple M4 chip is plenty fast. It works with the excellent Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil, and the 11-inch screen is better suited for productive tasks like editing, drawing, schoolwork, and more. It’s not a handheld gaming machine like the Astra 2, but it does almost everything else better. I tested the REDMAGIC Astra 2 for two months and pitted it against a handful of other tablets, including the iPad mini, the iPad Pro, and the OnePlus Pad 4. During the test period, I played a variety of native Android games as well as emulated titles on this tablet. For charging tests, I used a standard 100W brick with a USB-C to USB-C cable. Gaming sessions were conducted in a variety of places, including public parks on a sunny day, the sitting area of a heated coffee shop, and my own drawing room. To get the most accurate thermal readings, I tested the tablet without a case. Additionally, all the benchmarks and gaming tests were run across the Rise, Eco, Balanced, and Diablo modes, both with and without liquid cooling enabled. FAQs (Frequently Asked Questions) What’s the asking price of the tablet? The base model (12GB RAM + 256GB storage) costs $699, while the top-end trim (16GB RAM + 512GB storage) is priced at $799. What about the cooling tech, and does it work? The tablet comes equipped with a 12-layer cooling system that includes flowing liquid coolant, liquid metal, and a vapor chamber. Does it heat while charging and playing games simultaneously? The tablet supports bypass charging, which means the battery is cut off, so the tablet runs relatively cooler during top-up. How long does the battery last on a single charge? Does it support fast charging? The battery is expected to last anywhere between 8-9 hours of 60fps gaming, but the real-life mileage is about 30-45% lower than the rated figures. Is it available to buy in the US? Yeah, you can place the order directly from REDMAGIC’s global site.

item.title: REVIEW: HyperX Omen 35L review: A polished gaming PC for deep pockets
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The HyperX Omen 35L delivers a premium gaming PC experience, pairing a striking black-and-white styling, quiet operation, enthusiast-grade features, and excellent 4K gaming performance. Top-end configurations make the most sense, as entry-level models are expensive for the hardware. Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. HP’s HyperX Omen 35L is ambitious, and it’s hard not to be impressed by it in our maxed-out test guise with a Ryzen 9 9950X3D and Nvidia RTX 5080. From its monochrome design and extensive RGB lighting to its top-tier components, it checks the boxes enthusiasts are looking for. But when a PC is $6,211 like our test configuration, it raises the question of whether the Omen 35L’s blend of style, performance, and premium features is enough to justify a purchase, even if that's what high-end PCs cost right now. The HyperX Omen 35L’s black and white case stands out, looking refreshingly modern, even though parent company HP has used similar designs before. At 8.27 by 16.06 by 16.14 inches, it’s firmly in mid-tower territory. The metal case feels reassuringly solid and makes extensive use of tempered glass. Bright RGB fans shine through the front while many RGB-lit components are visible through the side panel. It’s a classy system. The contrast continues inside, where the black motherboard, graphics card, and power supply are easily visible against the white case. The white liquid cooling loops are especially attractive, as is the CPU cooler featuring its own LCD panel. The latter shows CPU and GPU temperatures. Ports and Upgradeability on the HyperX Omen 35L HyperX’s top-mounted front ports include USB-C (10 Gbps), two USB-A (5 Gbps), and an audio combo jack. This location works well if the desktop is on the floor. At the back, the tower offers a pair of USB-C ports (10 Gbps), two USB-A (5 Gbps), four USB 2.0, DisplayPort 1.4 output, Ethernet, and audio jacks. It’s disappointing to see a desktop this expensive offers neither USB4 nor Thunderbolt 4, though it does include Wi-iFi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0 from a Realtek 8922AE networking card. The wireless antennas are built into the chassis, eliminating the need for external protrusions. It’s also notable that HP offers a Clear CMOS button, a surprise on a mainstream tower. The HyperX Omen 35L offers about as much upgradeability as expected from a mid-tower, without proprietary parts. Its side doors are secured with thumbscrews; the slide rearward and away. The mATX-style motherboard offers four DDR5 DIMM slots, populated in our review unit with two 32GB RGB HyperX modules running at 6,000 MHz. The system also supports two M.2 2280 drives. The primary slot is covered in a substantial heatsink just above the RTX 5080. Accessing the other slot requires removing the RTX 5080. The card is secured with five screws, two of which hold it to the front support bracket. Deft fingers are required to reinstall the screws at the back of the card. HP’s wiring work is tidy for a mainstream tower. Sleeved cables would have improved the refinement. On the plus side, HP includes a fully modular power supply, an uncommon feature in big box systems. Gaming and Graphics on the HyperX Omen 35L We tested the HyperX Omen 35L in a maxed-out configuration featuring a Ryzen 9 9950X3D processor, 64GB of RAM, and a GeForce RTX 5080. I fired up 007 First Light to test out this system’s prowess. At a 3840 x 2160 resolution with high settings and post effects enabled, I saw up to 120 frames per second (fps) indoors and in the mid-90 fps range in more complex scenes without DLSS. The game never stuttered and remained supremely playable. The systems we’re using for comparison include a pair of RTX 5090 towers, the Alienware Area-51 (Ryzen 9950X3D, $5,749.99 when tested, $8,899.99 as of this writing) and the Maingear MG-1 (Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, $7,067 when tested, $9,076 as of this writing), plus Corsair’s Vengeance a7500 powered by a Ryzen 7 9800X3D and an RTX 5070 Ti ($2,799.99 when tested, $3,299.99 as of this writing). With its RTX 5080, the HyperX desktop ought to slot in the middle of this group. The HyperX desktop performed as expected given its RTX 5080. That said, the 1080p numbers show significant variance from system to system. In Shadow of the Tomb Raider (Highest detail preset), the HyperX produced 300 fps to outperform even the Alienware (248 fps), though it couldn’t catch the Maingear (355 fps). In other instances, even the RTX 5070-powered Corsair was able to pull ahead as seen in Far Cry 6 (Ultra settings), where it produced 197 fps against the HyperX’s 141 fps. But these desktops are designed for 4K play. At that resolution, the HyperX’s RTX 5080 produced admirable numbers. Naturally, it wasn’t in the same league as the RTX 5090 systems; in Red Dead Redemption 2 (Medium settings), the HyperX produced 83 fps against the Alienware’s 122 fps and the Maingear’s 121 fps, and in Borderlands 3 (Badass settings), the HyperX landed at 115 fps against Alienware’s 166 fps and Maingear’s 186 fps. The differences narrowed in Far Cry 6, with the HyperX producing 118 fps to Alienware’s 128 fps. The largest deltas were seen in Cyberpunk 2077 (Ray Tracing Ultra preset), where the HyperX produced 36 fps, well ahead of the Corsair’s 29 fps, but significantly behind the Alienware’s 55 fps. Overall, though, this HyperX desktop is well-suited to 4K play. We stress-test gaming desktops running 15 loops of the Metro Exodus benchmark at RTX settings, simulating about half an hour of gameplay. During the test, the HyperX desktop averaged 172.21 fps across all runs with a sub-one fps variance, indicating stable performance. During the test, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D averaged 4.79 GHz and 48 degrees Celsius while the RTX 5080 ran at 2.74 GHz and 50 C. Productivity Performance on the HyperX Omen 35L Our HyperX test unit features a Ryzen 9 9950X3D processor, 64GB of RAM, and two 1TB PCIe 5.0 drives running separately, one hosting the OS andthe other for storage. Featuring the same Ryzen 9 9950X3D processor, the HyperX and Alienware systems performed similarly across our CPU tests. In Geekbench 6, the HyperX system produced 19,923 points against Alienware’s 20,411 points, though it was handily outperformed by the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2-powered Maingear, at 23,741 points. With fewer cores, the Ryzen 7 9800X3D-powered Corsair finished last, at 18,124 points. The HyperX desktop finished our Handbrake 4K-to-1080p video transcoding test in 1 minute and 47 seconds, tying the Alienware, though the Maingear edged ahead, at 1:32. The Corsair took nearly twice as long, at 3:02. In our 25GB file transfer test, the HyperX’s average transfer speed of 3,197.42 MBps was excellent, just behind Alienware’s 3,414.29 MBps and ahead of the Corsair’s 2,659.94 MBps and Maingear’s 2,782.43 MBps. Software and Warranty on the HyperX Omen 35L HP includes several useful apps. Omen Gaming Hub app provides performance control, with per-fan RPM settings and, in Extreme mode, PPT and EDC settings for the Ryzen 9 CPU. The Advanced Performance Tuning section also provides PBO, CPU Boost, and voltage curve controls plus a benchmark to test your settings. For quick access, the app provides an overlay that shows your power profiles and system monitoring, including component temperatures and fan speeds. Gaming Hub also provides customization of the LCD display on the liquid cooler. Many faces are available, from system monitoring to static images, GIFs, videos, and a clock. It seems simple, but it’s one of the most fun features of the system, allowing you to easily change up the look. Lighting is managed through Omen Light Studio, which provides per-device RGB control. Fine control is possible – each of the five fans has 10 LEDs, which are individually selectable. Clicking and dragging selects multiple fans and LEDs at a time, to which you can apply preconfigured light recipes – Galaxy, Ocean, Jungle, Volcano, and Omen – and apply an effect, such as wave, static, ambient, breathing, color cycle, an audio visualizer, and radial. The speed and direction of the effect is also configurable. You can also create layered effects and save everything in profiles that you can export or import. HP covers the HyperX Omen 35L with a standard one-year warranty. We tested the HyperX Omen 35L with a Ryzen 9 9950X3D processor, 64GB of dual-channel DDR5-6000 RAM, GeForce RTX 5080 graphics, Windows 11 Pro, and two 1TB PCIe 5.0 solid-state drives. The system uses a 1,000W power supply and a 240 mm liquid CPU cooling with a built-in LCD display. This configuration represents the top of the stack, retailing for $6,210.98. The entry-level is probably where the Omen 35L offers the least value – with standard liquid cooling and a modular power supply, this system is for premium builds. AMD-based starter configurations begin at $2,399.99 with a Ryzen 5 9600X or $2,589.99 with an Intel Core Ultra 5 250KF Plus. Standard components include a GeForce RTX 5060 Ti (8GB), 16GB of memory, and 1TB of PCIe 4.0 storage. Memory tops out at 128GB and two SSDs are supported up to 2TB each. Primarily, the HyperX Omen 35L gets one thing right: it feels genuinely premium. Its sharp black-and-white design, quality lighting, quiet operation, and enthusiast-grade components like a modular power supply give it the polish it needs to compete against boutique builders and aftermarket systems. Its performance in our test system with a Ryzen 9 9950X3D and an RTX 5080 match the expectations for this lofty price point. That said, it’s clear that this desktop is aimed at the more premium side of the market, as prices of the entry-level configurations are difficult to justify given their level of hardware. But if you have deep enough pockets for a well-equipped configuration, the HyperX Omen 35L is a highly compelling gaming desktop well worth considering alongside anything the market has to offer.

Note that the company no longer targets the average user, but I found that it works exceptionally well even on a single computer. - Handy Backup Professional: Top-notch features that might’ve garnered a higher rating had it been entirely glitch-free and a bit easier to learn. - NTI Backup Now Pro 7: Another suite that offers a strong feature set — file backup, imaging, continuous and cloud backup — yet is tarnished by glitches. - Ashampoo Backup Pro 27: A great total backup solution for the average user, but a couple features shy of being “pro.” - Paragon Backup & Recovery Community Edition: A free program that offers robust file backup that should meet the needs of most users. - Perfect Backup: Fast and competent, this free backup program is more versatile than Windows File History. - Aomei Backupper Pro: A complete backup solution capable of preserving your important data both locally and remotely. - Aomei Backupper Standard: A respectable free backup program if you can tolerate the occasional ad. - Retrospect 19 Solo: Includes support for both proprietary and third-party cloud storage, but sadly it lacks disaster recovery. - Retrospect 19 Desktop: The pro version of the above covers all the bases, but has a steep learning curve and high price. - Backup and Restore (Windows 7): Conveniently installed with Windows, and good for imaging but bad for disaster recover. - MSP360 Managed Backup: Uses a handy web-based console to provide imaging and file backup services for multiple devices at a reasonable price. - MSP360 Backup: The free incarnation is a worthwhile upgrade to Windows File History. - Iperius Backup: Has power aplenty, but the learning curve and interface might occasionally flummox less-experienced users. - MiniTool ShadowMaker Pro 4.6: There’s a lot to like, particularly its unique ability to interface with all computers on a network. - Macrium Reflect Home: Would likely qualify as our favorite backup software if it wasn’t relatively pricey. It’s an exceptional program that offers everything we want from backup software — full drive/folder backup, ease of use, reliability, etc. - DriveImage XML: A viable free backup solution, albeit only for MBR disks. Note that in this article we focus on local-software based solutions, although many also include a cloud component. For cloud-first backup, see our roundup of the best online backup services. Admittedly, the distinction between the two categories is blurring as they each expand their feature sets. Our reviewers run each program through the various types of backups and restores it’s capable of — including those requiring boot media. This is largely to gauge reliability and hardware compatibility. We check speed, but such is highly reliant upon the connections and media involved. If we notice anything is particularly fast or slow, we’ll tell you about it, but creating a functional backup is paramount. To learn more details, see our article on how PCWorld tests backup software. Having started computing by flipping switches, Jon Jacobi has witnessed storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for well over two decades. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two. If you recently purchased an external HDD or SSD from a major vendor such as Seagate or WD, check to see if there are backup utilities or a backup software license included. Whatever backup software you use, keep in mind the following key aspects of the best solutions: file backup for documents/photos, image backup for whole-PC rollback, boot media for dead-drive recovery, versioning for accidental overwrite protection, and know which are critical to your backup plan. If you want to back up your essential data (operating systems and programs can be reinstalled, though it’s mildly time- and effort-consuming), a program that backs up only your important files is essential. Some programs even automatically select the appropriate files or folders. File backup can include operating system files if you wish but is still not suitable for disaster recovery. Images are byte-for-byte snapshots of your entire hard drive (normally not including empty sectors) or partitions, and can be used to restore the operating system, drivers, programs in one swift, fell swoop. Imaging also ensures that you don’t omit anything important as can happen with file backup. Should your system crash completely, you need alternate means to boot your system and restore data using your backup software. Any backup program worth its salt should be able to create a bootable optical disc or USB thumb drive. Some will also create a restore partition on your hard drive, which can be used if the issue isn’t a failed drive. Note that we’ve run into multiple issues with Microsoft’s own Recovery Drive and System repair disc — don’t rely on those. If you’re going to back up effectively, you need to do so on a regular basis. Any backup program you purchase should let you schedule backups and run them in the background. Some even will backup files as they change (real time) or at very short intervals (continuous) Versioning is simply retaining older version of files (or backups) rather than overwriting them during the backup/sync process. You can generally define how many versions to keep, but if you choose to cull older files, this is till not true backup which again, is an immutable copy of your data, drives, or system. Every backup program supports hard drives, but as obsolete as they may seem, DVDs and Blu-Ray discs are great archive media. If you’re worried about optical media’s reliability, M-Disc claims its discs are reliable for a thousand years, backed up by Department of Defense testing. An offsite copy of your data is a hedge against physical disasters such as theft, flood, fire, and power surges. Online storage services are a great way to meet that need. Some backup software will let you back up to Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, Amazon S3 and compatible, etc. however Cloud Managers can serve as a workaround with backup programs that don’t. The downside to cloud storage is relatively slow performance. Keep a local backup for faster restores. Backing up to other computers or NAS boxes on your network or in remote locations (say your parent’s or children’s house) is another way of safeguarding your data via a physically remote copy. If you use network storage, it can also be handy to back them up to you local system. FTP/SFTP can be used for offsite, while SMB (Windows and most OS’s) and AFP (Apple) are good for other PCs or NAS on your local network. Network support is not universal, and some backup programs allow you to back up to, but not from network shares. Just be careful in the way you expose your computers on the Internet. Real-time backup means that files are backed up whenever they change, usually upon creation or save. It’s handy for keeping an immediately available backup of rapidly changing data sets. For less volatile data sets, scheduled backups will do just fine. Continuous simply means backing up on a tight schedule, generally every few minutes, rather than in real time, daily, weekly, or monthly. Use continuous backup for rapidly changing data sets where transfer rates are too slow, or computing power too precious for real-time backup. Most backups proceed in the background or during dead time, so performance isn’t a huge issue in the consumer space. However, if you’re backing up multiple machines, backing up to multiple destinations, or dealing with very large data sets, speed will be a consideration. That said, backup speed is highly dependent upon the hardware and transport technology in use. Further reading: Check out PCWorld’s roundup of best external drives for recommendations on reliable storage options — an important component in a comprehensive backup strategy. What is the best Windows backup software? The best Windows backup software is Easeus Todo Backup 2025. It has everything PCWorld expects to see in a top product: A polished interface, intuitive functionality, a comprehensive approach to backing up data including imaging, file backup, sync, and disaster recovery. And most important, it’s reliable! Todo Backup also offers the option of a perpetual license or a subscription model, the latter of which can be augmented with affordable cloud storage. What is the best free Windows backup software? It turns out that PCWorld’s favorite for-pay backup software, Easeus Todo Backup 2025, also offers a surprisingly robust free version. It matches its paid counterpart in basics such as imaging, file backup, sync, and, most especially — disaster recovery. It also features the same eminently user-friendly interface. As with most backup freeware, you will be nagged to upgrade, and Easeus’s optional cloud storage, which is surprisingly affordable, is only available at the subscription tier. Will backup software slow down my computer? Backup software typically runs in the background or during dead time, so given even moderately modern hardware, you shouldn’t notice any decrease in performance. Most programs let you throttle the backup process if you do notice a slowdown. Does Windows Backup and Restore (Windows 7) save everything? Yes, by default, Backup and Restore (Windows 7) saves everything on your system disk (all the partitions, including hidden ones) in what’s known as an image file that would be suitable for disaster recovery if Windows Recovery Drive and Rescue disk were reliable. News bulletin — they aren’t. Hence, we only recommend this program for creating highly compatible VHD/VHDX images of your data drives and partitions which can be mounted as virtual drives and browsed using nothing but Windows Explorer. What’s the difference between Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, etc. and backup software? Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive are what’s known as cloud storage, or online storage. They create a local virtual drive that you can drag files to, and which is eventually synced to the cloud as time allows. They also provide a Web portal where you can manage your files remotely. However, by default these services sync changes in the data across all devices. True backups should be immutable snapshots that may be added to but not changed. Some services offer versioning (keeping older files, and adding new ones), which creates a close approximation to backup. Cloud backup services (distinct from those mentioned above) offer many, though not all, of the benefits of Windows backup software. This is generally done with local client software that offers just basic functions like file backup and sync. You can learn more about these in our roundup of best cloud backup services. How often should backups be scheduled? Ideally, as often as your data changes. If you are working on an important project or have work that you absolutely cannot afford to lose, you should consider real time (as data changes) or continuous (very short intervals). Hourly, daily, or longer intervals will be fine for the average user. All file backups should be augmented by weekly or monthly system backups. Can I back up files to and from my cloud storage? Until a few years ago, most Windows backup software was restricted to making local backups — i.e., to another drive, external or internal, connected to your system. There were of course services such as Mozy that had their own backup clients, but that’s covered in our online backup roundup. Here we’re talking just plain backup programs. The situation is improving rapidly, and many backup software vendors are adding online storage services as destinations for their backups. If your favorite backup program doesn’t support cloud storage directly, a cloud storage manager that integrates online storage services into File Explorer can make online backup possible with just about any backup app. What’s the difference between full, differential, and incremental backup? A full backup is a backup of all your data, regardless of how new or old it is. A differential backup is all the data that’s changed since your last full backup. An incremental backup is all the data that’s changed since any your original full and/or the last differential/incremental backup. Differential and incremental backups require a initial full backup to be restored. Differential backups require more time to create than incremental backups, but are quicker to restore since you only need the latest iteration. Differential backups can grow to be quite large if you don’t perform full backups very often. Incremental backups take less time to produce and are smaller, but take longer to restore as all of them created since the last full backup must be restored in the order in which they were created. What’s the difference between image backup, system backup, and file backup? An image is low-level backup of all the sectors (including “empty” sectors if you wish) contained by a disk or partition, regardless of their pertinence to your files. It’s basically fool-proof in terms of accidentally overlooking important data. A system backup is an disk image backup of all the partitions on your system drive. This includes several that are hidden, i.e., not enumerated as drive letters by the operating system. A system backup might also include other drives, but must contain the OS drive. A file backup is a high-level backup of data read via the operating system’s file system. Most often this is data, but may include all the files on a drive. What should I back up? In truth, it’s only your essential personal data that must absolutely, positively, 100% be backed up. Once the family pictures or your work-in-progress are trashed with no backup, there’s no way back other than an expensive recovery service, and even that’s not guaranteed if the physical media is unreadable. On the other hand, a system backup is exceedingly handy for getting you back up to speed with minimal hassle. It returns your system to exactly where you were at the time of the backup: OS, program, updates, upgrades, settings, data are all back in a relative blink of the eye. But it’s not essential. While reinstalling operating systems, drivers, and programs, as well as adjusting settings require more effort, you can then recover your data if that’s all you backed up. See the first paragraph.

item.title: SALES: Where to Stay in Big Sky, Montana, When You’re Dreaming of the Wild West
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
I’ve visited Big Sky, Montana, a handful of times over the past six years, and I’m still completely smitten. This corner of the Rockies, roughly 45 miles south of Bozeman, is a choose-your-own-adventure kind of city. Winter ski days beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak give way to summer rafting trips and fly-fishing on the Gallatin River, while fall brings horseback rides that sprawl across open ranchlands, and spring offers hikes through wildflower-strewn meadows. The iconic Yellowstone National Park is about an hour south too, putting geysers, steaming hot springs, and roaming bison within day-tripping distance. The city itself is a quaint yet buzzy collection of restaurants, shops, and watering holes, all adding a welcome dose of small-town charm to all that wilderness. And lately, the destination’s hospitality scene has been booming, with a new wave of stylish hotels and mountain retreats bringing some fresh takes to the city’s rugged Western roots. From luxe resorts with front-row views of the towering peaks to authentic dude ranches and design-forward Airbnbs with cozy fireplaces, there’s an accommodation for every style of Big Sky getaway on the list below. Read on for the best places to stay in Montana’s sweet mountain hub. - Read Full ReviewNumber of guests: Varies Why we love it: Mountain access, gorgeous standalone cabins, private hot tubs, spa and wellness facilities (with indoor-outdoor lap pool, heated onsen soaking tub, cold plunge, steam room, and sauna)Famed for its sumptuous yet tasteful resorts in far-flung destinations like Mauritius, Rwanda, and Malaysia, One&Only’s 2025 Moonlight Basin opening was the brand's American debut, as well as its first foray into the outdoor adventure space. A luxury alpine retreat like this requires a specialized type of hospitality, and the team here—a crew who can do everything from book your activities to whisk you between buildings on a side-by-side ATV—knows exactly what they’re doing. Guests get a direct line to the slopes via the One&Only gondola, as well as access to plush locker rooms, tuning equipment, and gear rentals that will impress even members of Yellowstone Club (the famously tiny private ski community next door). Moonlight Basin is worth visiting outside of ski season too. Situated on 240 secluded acres within the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, the resort links two sections of protected wilderness in southwestern Montana’s Rocky Mountains, providing critical migration routes for species like moose and bobcats, which means you're in for some exceptional wildlife sightings. Add fly-fishing, stargazing at the on-site observatory, and unwinding at the 17,000-square-foot spa, and even the most discerning ski bums will find themselves spoiled rotten. —Hannah Towey Neighborhood: Moonlight Basin Things to do nearby: Lone Peak, Madison River Valley, Big Sky Mountain, Madison Base Area Why we love it: White-glove service, buzzy après bar, full spa, on-site activity center, ski-in/ski-out locationMontage Big Sky has always been more rugged than refined, but the buzz around this slopeside resort has Aspen and Jackson Hole loyalists rethinking their next ski vacation. The first five-star resort in Big Sky ushered in a whole new era of luxury for this mountain destination, with an 11,000-square-foot spa (the first true spa in the region), a buzzy bar scene, and stellar restaurants. Most of the 139 rooms, suites, and residences have terraces and balconies with mountain views, and gas fireplaces turn on with a flip of a switch. Head to Beartooth Pub & Rec for a menu of comfort foods, like Wagyu nachos and oversized hot pretzels served alongside cold-smoked beer-cheese dip. —Jen Murphy Neighborhood: Spanish Peaks Things to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Ousel Falls Trail, Lone Peak, Beehive Basin Trail, Gallatin and Madison Rivers Why we love it: True dude ranch experience, tasteful cabin design, horseback riding experiences for all levels, easy access to townLone Mountain Ranch, one of Montana’s longest-standing dude ranches, has plenty going for it: a wonderfully attentive staff, character-filled cabins, and a calendar of special events that draw in both longtime regulars and first-time horseback riders. The on-site wranglers are happy to work with riders of all levels one-on-one, even if that means helping you get past a few preexisting fears before climbing into the saddle. The ranch’s roots reach back to the early days of Yellowstone, with its owners involved in conversations around Big Sky’s formation and the region’s ranching, logging, and wilderness preservation. Yet unlike many of Montana’s more remote ranches, it’s conveniently less than a 10-minute drive from town. You may still find little reason to leave: Set among towering aspens, the 150-acre guest ranch has 25 restored historic cabins, each with its own Wild West–inspired name and one to six bedrooms. And then there are the signature experiences, including Cowgirl Up, a weeklong retreat that brings women from around the world together to experience ranch life and release their inner cowgirl. Neighborhood: Lone Mountain Things to do nearby: Big Sky Town Center, Ousel Falls Trail, Moonlight Basin, Gallatin River, Big Sky Resort Why we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, gas fireplace, mountain views, outdoor seating on the patioThere’s something pretty splendid about staying at 8,300 feet, especially when the mountains are quite literally at your doorstep. This standalone cabin in Big Sky’s (iconically named) Cowboy Heaven neighborhood is a haven for folks who wish to spend their days outside, whether that means skiing straight from the deck in the winter or taking advantage of the area’s hiking and wildlife spotting in the warmer months. It’s especially ideal for couples, small families, or friend groups, with one caveat for your crew: The second bedroom has a queen-over-twin bunk, so five adults looking for equal amounts of space may want to look elsewhere. A big plus? The town center is less than a 10-minute drive away. Neighborhood: Cowboy Heaven Things to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Lone Mountain, Moonlight Lodge, Big Sky Town Center Why we love it: Private hot tub, in-unit washer and dryer, indoor wood-burning fireplace, fully equipped kitchen, patio with outdoor furniture, longer stays allowedWith three floors and two separate living areas, this Big Sky rental gives small groups room to spread out between outings. And there’s plenty to get out for: Big Sky Resort is about 1.2 miles away, Beehive Basin Trailhead is roughly 2.6 miles, and Ousel Falls Park is another nearby option for low-key but scenic walks. Inside the light-filled abode, fun Western touches are everywhere. In true Big Sky fashion, you’ll find everything from hanging longhorns and antlers to framed photographs of bison and horses. Through a wall of windows, you can look past the cozy fireplace into the hilly woods—the towering trees are gorgeous year-round. Do note this base might be best for four, rather than six, despite what the listing says. There are two generously sized bedrooms, but two sofa beds in the living room.
